title: The croissant's Austrian roots
hook: France's most famous pastry started out as a Viennese crescent roll.
peek: The croissant is a symbol of French baking, but its ancestor is the Austrian kipferl, a crescent bread. An Austrian baker in 1830s Paris helped bring it over, and French bakers later made it flaky.
lede: The croissant feels as French as anything gets, yet its ancestor is the kipferl, a crescent-shaped bread baked in Austria for centuries. In the late 1830s, a former Austrian army officer named August Zang opened a Viennese bakery in Paris. His kipferl and other Viennese breads caught on, and French bakers made the shape their own.

bullets.text: Zang's bakery gave French a word that is still on bakery signs: viennoiserie, meaning Viennese-style goods. It covers croissants, pains au chocolat and brioche, the rich breads between bread and pastry.
The flaky croissant is a French refinement. Bakers fold butter into the dough again and again to build thin layers, and recipes for this version appear in the early 20th century.

A popular story says Viennese bakers invented the crescent to celebrate beating the Ottoman army in 1683. Historians doubt it: crescent breads existed in Austria well before then, and the tale appears much later.
Another legend credits the Austrian-born queen with bringing the croissant to France. There is no good evidence for it, and the pastry as we know it came long after her time.
